title: Cheyenne Wells Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cheyenne Wells wells have a 326-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $17,400-$29,900.
intro_html:
Buying land near Cheyenne Wells means evaluating the well as carefully as the house, road, and septic system. Records for permitted wells within the Cheyenne Wells area show a generally productive plains setting, but the available information is uneven: 210 wells appear in Colorado DWR records, while only 59 are recorded as constructed and 12 report a static water level.

The numbers below help set expectations for depth, water production, drilling cost, and due diligence. They are not a guarantee for an untested lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact parcel, access, geology, intended use, casing and grout requirements, and the applicable DWR permit conditions.

sections.heading: Cheyenne Wells wells usually reach the deeper plains formations
sections.html:
Reported well depth has a median of 326 feet. The middle half runs from 285 to 390 feet, so a bid based on a shallow well would not fit the local record very well. The deepest reported well is 464 feet, and 69% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet. Only 1% are under 100 feet.

That depth pattern matches a plains setting with alluvium and sedimentary rock rather than a uniformly shallow water source. The aquifer names in the records include the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer and the Ogallala. A driller should explain which formation is expected at a particular lot, along with the casing and grout plan.

sections.heading: Cheyenne Wells production is generally better than a marginal household well
sections.html:
Among the 64 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 20.5 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 14.8 to 42.5 gallons per minute. That is a useful starting point for a rural home, livestock operation, or irrigation discussion, but it is not a promise for a new hole.

Seventy-five percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 22% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the actual pump test, recovery information, and intended-use permit rather than relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Cheyenne Wells water levels need parcel-specific checking
sections.html:
Only 12 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. For those wells, the median depth to water is 246 feet, with the middle half from 204 to 287 feet. That gives a reasonable planning signal for drilling and pump placement, but it is not a complete groundwater map.

The permit counts by decade do not show a water-table trend. They show activity, not measured water levels: permits range from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2024. Before buying, compare nearby well construction reports and static levels, then have a driller evaluate the lot. The Ogallala and unnamed or fractured-bedrock records can behave differently from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Permit history points to established local drilling experience
sections.html:
Cheyenne Wells has a long permit history, with records dating from the 1950s through the 2020s. The busiest period in the available list is the 1970s, with 33 permits. There are also 27 permits in the 2000s, 26 in the 1990s, and 11 in the 2020s. A recent permit exists from 2024.

The most active driller in these records is Kemp's Well Service (Kemp, George), associated with 53 wells. Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) appears on 10, and Dmw Well & Pump Service (Hudnell, Jerry T.) on 7. Treat this as permit history, not a current recommendation or a guarantee of availability.

sections.heading: A median-depth Cheyenne Wells project needs a realistic budget
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the median depth of 326 feet, drilling alone is estimated at about $11,400 to $17,900, using a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. That is the drilled hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $17,400 to $29,900. The final bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, formation conditions, pump size, power distance, and whether the hole must go deeper. When comparing bids, ask what is included and what happens if the hole does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield, septic space, and buildability
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 30 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it does justify a site-specific water test and a review of nearby land uses. Historic mine features are not mapped in the area.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk cannot be eliminated by an area median. Confirm the well permit, construction report, pump test, static level, and water-quality history before closing. Also verify that the lot has adequate room for the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house. DWR rules control the well use; an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cheyenne Wells?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Cheyenne Wells is 326 feet. The middle half runs from 285 to 390 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 464 feet. Most wells are in the 300-to-600-foot range. These figures are planning benchmarks, not a guarantee for a particular parcel, because local formations and the intended well location still matter.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Cheyenne Wells?
faq.a: At the local median depth of 326 feet, the estimated drilled-hole cost is $11,400-$17,900. A finished system with a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $17,400-$29,900. The final price depends on access, casing and grout, pump equipment, power distance, formation conditions, and whether additional drilling is required.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Cheyenne Wells?
faq.a: Among 64 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 20.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 14.8-42.5 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those results are encouraging, but a buyer should obtain the specific well's pump test and recovery information instead of applying the area median to an untested lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Cheyenne Wells?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Records map 30 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not prove a problem at your property. Test the well water for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest after construction or changes in water quality.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Cheyenne Wells?
faq.a: Verify the Colorado DWR permit, construction report, well depth, pump yield, static water level, and water-quality history. The local records show a 326-foot median depth, but only 12 wells report static levels, so parcel-specific information matters. Also confirm septic and replacement-area space, driveway access, electrical needs, and whether the intended use has the required water rights or augmentation arrangement.
